paras: The whipping of Clarence Cooper was an attack on a Black landowner by a group of white men outside his church in Homer, Louisiana, on a Sunday in early March 1919. Cooper had sold his land and announced that he was moving North, and his attackers whipped him into insensibility and then told the congregation it was a warning to anyone else who left. The only known report, in the Phoenix Tribune, said the United States Department of Justice was being asked to investigate.
According to the Tribune's Homer item, oil wells sunk among the town's Black residents had made many Black families wealthy through the sale or lease of their farms.

Clarence Cooper sold his land "at the top price" and let it be known that he was leaving for the North, where, the paper said, he hoped to raise and educate his children without "the restrictions of prejudice and the fear of injustice and mob violence."

On the Sunday before the paper's March 8 issue, as Cooper was about to enter his church, "a group of brutal and fendish white Louisianians" stopped him. They whipped him "into insensibility" in front of the church. The men then went into the church, boasted of what they had done, and called it a warning to any others "who dared to leave the place in search of other conditions."

The Tribune reported that the Department of Justice was "being appealed to" to investigate and to protect Black residents against what it called an "open violation of their Constitutional rights." No report of arrests, a federal inquiry or Cooper's recovery appears in the coverage.

The Phoenix Tribune printed the story on its front page on March 8, 1919, under the headline "Colored Man Received Brutal Treatment in Louisiana." The item named the attackers only by race, called their act "inhuman and Hunnish," and opened with the Liberty bond purchases of Homer's Black residents, one of whom had invested $100,000. It framed the whipping as a blow against the right of Black Southerners to move North and as a matter for federal authorities.

reader.title: Whipping of Clarence Cooper
bases: A group of white men stopped and whipped one Black man in public outside his church and then announced it as a warning to others who meant to leave; no organized night band, notice to leave, or killing is reported (A1).
Only one Black-press item reports the whipping, and no other paper or follow-up was found (A1).
